talks.title: Attack Trends in 2022
talks.teaser: An analysis of prominent cyberattack vectors, adversary tradecraft shifts, and ransomware trends observed across 2022.
talks.summary:
In this virtual presentation hosted in AltspaceVR for the DEF CON 30 DCGVR track, Jon Clay, VP of Threat Intelligence at Trend Micro, provides an analysis of the cyber attack landscape in 2022. He opens at 07:00 by mapping the evolution of threat actors, contrasting entry-level script kiddies with organized ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) cartels and nation-state advanced persistent threats.

Jon analyzes modern adversary tradecraft at 14:00, explaining the proliferation of initial access brokers (IABs) on underground forums and the tactics attackers use to move laterally into cloud infrastructure. At 21:00, he examines how threat groups continually tweak code to evade endpoint detection systems and heavily exploit living-off-the-land binaries already present on victim systems.

Highlighting rapid exploit weaponization at 28:00, Jon warns that the window between vulnerability disclosure and automated in-the-wild exploitation has collapsed to hours. He advocates for modern security operations at 35:00, urging organizations to adopt continuous Attack Surface Management (ASM) and discovery frameworks to identify exposed assets before adversaries do. He closes at 42:00 with questions from the virtual reality audience. (AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: Exploits & Dragons: Gamifying Infosec Education with Tabletop RPGs
talks.teaser: Exploits & Dragons explores how tabletop roleplaying game mechanics can be used to simulate cyber attacks, incident response, and threat modeling.
talks.summary:
Security researchers and founders from DEF CON group DC5411 (Argentina and Uruguay) present "Exploits & Dragons," an innovative initiative that gamifies cybersecurity education and incident response training using tabletop role-playing games (RPGs).

[01:27] The speakers discuss how traditional security awareness training and technical workshops often struggle to engage participants. In response, they designed "Exploits & Dragons," adapting tabletop role-playing mechanics (similar to Dungeons & Dragons) to represent computer networks, defensive controls, threat actors, and digital vulnerabilities in a collaborative narrative setting.

[04:30] The presentation walks through character archetypes, game scenarios, and quest structures where players utilize real-world infosec skills—such as network reconnaissance, threat modeling, and incident containment—to overcome challenges. The speakers demonstrate how custom templates [19:05], quest-based scoring, and hands-on tabletop storytelling foster critical thinking, teamwork, and deeper technical comprehension for newcomers and experienced security professionals alike.

talks.title: Ham Radio is Not Just for Dinosaurs
talks.teaser: Demystifying amateur radio for modern hackers, exploring digital packet radio, APRS telemetry, SDR integration, and emergency communications.
talks.summary:
In this virtual session for DEF CON 30 DCGVR hosted in AltspaceVR, Giglio and fellow DEF CON organizers deliver "Ham Radio is Not Just for Dinosaurs," debunking dated misconceptions about amateur radio and showcasing its modern technological relevance for hackers. He begins at 04:00 by highlighting how contemporary amateur radio has evolved into a vibrant testing ground for digital communications, high-altitude ballooning, and satellite telemetry.

Giglio introduces accessible hardware at 12:00, explaining how inexpensive Software-Defined Radio (SDR) USB dongles allow beginners to listen to aircraft transponders, weather satellites, and emergency services across hundreds of megahertz without expensive equipment. At 16:00, he explores amateur packet radio, digital weak-signal modes like FT8, and off-grid emergency mesh communications such as the Amateur Radio Emergency Data Network (AREDN).

The session outlines the licensing process at 20:00, providing guidance on studying for FCC technician license exams with resources from the ARRL and joining local amateur radio clubs. Giglio wraps up at 24:00 by encouraging virtual attendees to experiment with RF technology, emphasizing that amateur radio licenses provide hackers with unique legal privileges to transmit high-power signals on experimental frequencies. talks.title: How My High School Creative Writing Class Prepared Me for Social Engineering
talks.teaser: Exploring how storytelling, character development, and narrative pacing learned in creative writing form the foundation of compelling social engineering pretexts.
talks.summary:
In this engaging presentation hosted in the DEF CON 30 virtual altspace, the speaker illustrates how principles learned in high school creative writing classes directly translate into advanced tradecraft for social engineering and tabletop exercise facilitation.

[10:39] The speaker explores the core literary elements of storytelling—genre, setting, character backstory, and dialogue tone—demonstrating how social engineers use these exact concepts to craft convincing pretexts and realistic personas. She explains that effective social engineering relies on establishing believable narratives that resonate with a target's expectations, emotional triggers, and organizational reality.

[21:21] The talk expands on applying creative writing to incident response tabletop simulations. The speaker explains how scenario design, narrative pacing, escalating conflict, and multi-threaded plot twists [31:55] transform boring compliance exercises into immersive, high-stakes simulations that genuinely test an organization's crisis decision-making. She concludes with practical advice on debriefing participants [43:06], using detailed observational notes to provide actionable feedback and strengthen organizational resilience.

talks.title: How Getting a Free Phone Got Me to Report Critical Vulnerabilities
talks.teaser: The journey of reverse engineering a budget Android smartphone, uncovering pre-installed carrier bloatware vulnerabilities and navigating responsible disclosure.
talks.summary:
In this presentation for DEF CON 30 DCGVR, mobile security researcher Jonathan Bar Or details how inspecting a complimentary Android smartphone led to the discovery of critical vulnerabilities in pre-installed carrier diagnostic applications. He begins at 08:00 by analyzing the security implications of Android WebViews, explaining the extreme risk of granting embedded web views native JavaScript interfaces without strict domain restrictions.

Jonathan walks through reverse engineering the device's pre-installed Device Health companion app at 16:00, identifying exported Android activities and internal IPC response handlers that failed to enforce origin validation. At 24:00, he demonstrates how an unprivileged local application or malicious webpage could trigger the Device Health browser activity through crafted intents to access restricted operating system functions.

Diving deeper into Android IPC mechanisms at 32:00, Jonathan illustrates how arbitrary input parameters passed through WebViews allowed command injection into native privileged daemon services at 40:00. He concludes at 48:00 by recounting the coordinated vulnerability disclosure process, contrasting proactive carriers that remediated the issues promptly with vendors that required extensive proof-of-concept demonstrations before acknowledging severe risk to millions of deployed devices. talks.title: Security Concerns of the Medical Laboratory
talks.teaser: An inside look at vulnerabilities in clinical laboratory automation, analyzing unauthenticated analyzer instruments, legacy LIMS software, and patient data risks.
talks.summary:
Clinical laboratory scientist and security researcher Squiddy sheds light on the frequently overlooked cybersecurity and operational risks within hospital and reference diagnostic medical laboratories.

[05:39] Squiddy contrasts traditional healthcare enterprise IT with the operational realities of the clinical laboratory, examining how Laboratory Information Systems (LIS) interact with high-throughput diagnostic instrumentation (such as automated hematology, clinical chemistry, and pathology analyzers). She describes cultural vulnerabilities in lab workflows, including high staff turnover, shared generic workstation logins, and the routine sharing of credentials among rotating technicians [11:15] racing to process critical patient samples under tight turnaround deadlines.

[17:29] The presentation highlights severe technical vulnerabilities in medical laboratory environments, noting that expensive diagnostic machines often run outdated, unsupported Windows operating systems with unpatched embedded controllers. Squiddy warns that while direct ransomware disruptions are dangerous, the subtler and more catastrophic threat is unauthorized data tampering—where malicious actors or human errors alter quantitative lab values (such as blood glucose, potassium, or troponin levels) in transit, leading clinicians to make fatal diagnostic and treatment decisions.

talks.title: When Firefox Gets Angry: Fuzzing & Exploiting Gecko Engine Internals
talks.teaser: Dissecting the internals of Mozilla Firefox's Gecko rendering engine, exploring DOM fuzzing methodologies and memory corruption vulnerability classes.
talks.summary:
In this presentation for DEF CON Group DCG 201 delivered in virtual reality at DEF CON 30 DCGVR, Sidepocket explores advanced browser DOM inspection techniques, developer tools, and client-side web exploitation. At 14:00, he demonstrates how to leverage browser developer tools to inspect dynamic elements, monitor network events, and extract client-side application state during open-source intelligence (OSINT) investigations.

Sidepocket highlights integrating external code editors at 28:00, showing how dumping complex DOM structures and obfuscated scripts directly into Sublime Text accelerates reverse engineering. At 42:00, he demonstrates an OSINT workflow for unmasking automated Twitter bot swarms ("spot the bot"), analyzing behavioral anomalies and synchronized posting intervals.

Moving into web application analysis at 56:00, Sidepocket shows techniques for multi-tab reconnaissance to audit third-party tracking scripts. At 01:10:00, he reveals methods for recovering hidden form elements, disabled password fields, and client-side validation logic. He wraps up at 01:24:00 with announcements regarding upcoming in-person meetings for DEF CON Group DCG 201 in New Jersey. (AI summary — Gemini Flash)
